title: A higher wage floor can change a factory's technology choice before worker outcomes are known
source_unit: Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies working paper using state-level robot exposure and plant-level industrial-robot imports linked to Census microdata
geography: United States manufacturing plants and state-border wage-floor comparisons

denominator.unit: study-defined manufacturing plants and robot-adoption outcomes; exact public abstract denominator not disclosed

minimum_wage_robot_adoption.unit: approximately percent increase in robot adoption relative to the mean for a 10 percent increase in the minimum wage

policy_to_technology_path.value: higher minimum wages raise the likelihood that manufacturing firms adopt robots
policy_to_technology_path.unit: reported relationship under the paper's preferred identification

worker_outcomes.value: not established by the public abstract
worker_outcomes.unit: employment, wages, hours, job quality, bargaining power, and household security

observations.method: Census CES working paper using state-level measures of robot exposure and plant-level industrial-robot import data linked to U.S. Census microdata from 1992-2021. The preferred design uses discontinuities at state borders to compare otherwise similar firms facing different wage floors.
observations.uncertainty: This is a working paper. The public page gives the main estimate but not the full sample construction, mechanisms, subgroup estimates, employment effects, or worker-level outcomes. Robot adoption is not the same as worker displacement, wage improvement, productivity, safety, or control over work.
observations.subgroup: Manufacturing plants exposed to different state minimum-wage floors, with state-level robot exposure and plant-level import measures; exact public subgroup counts are not disclosed.
observations.counterinterpretation: Firms can respond to a higher wage floor through automation, prices, hours, hiring, product mix, outsourcing, relocation, or retention. Robots can replace some tasks, complement workers, improve safety, or increase output. State-border designs reduce some confounding but do not by themselves show the full distribution of gains and losses across workers, places, or households.

related_sources.claim: The Census working-paper catalog lists CES-26-42 and summarizes its minimum-wage and robot-adoption estimate.

boundary: This record adds a bounded policy-to-firm-technology relationship. It does not establish net employment loss, worker wage effects, household welfare, regional decline, political response, or whether automation increased or reduced practical worker control.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Census CES-26-42 landing page and official working-paper catalog reviewed; underlying restricted microdata and paper PDF are not retained
